hook.support: Is there something in your town that should change? A broken skate park? No bus at night? You can run a campaign. Make your case. Get people on board.

In this capstone, you’ll pick a local issue and build a mini campaign: a clear argument, a post that spreads it, and a short speech that makes people act.
hook.extend: Change in a community usually comes from a campaign. That means organised advocacy, kept up over time. It joins evidence, a clear ask and different texts for different audiences. In this capstone, you’ll run a mini campaign on a local issue. You’ll write an argument, make a post and give a speech.

articles.title: How campaigns win

body.support:
A **campaign** is a plan to make a change. You can run one about something in your town.

**1. Pick an issue.** Choose something real and local.
- no lights at the skate park.
- no bus after 7 pm.
- rubbish in the creek.

**2. Make a clear ask.** Say exactly what should change. “Two lights at the skate park.”

**3. Find who decides.** Is it the council? The school? A club?

**4. Get evidence.** Take photos. Count things. Ask people.

**5. Make three texts:**
- **An argument:** a letter to the person who decides.
- **A post:** to get people to sign or share.
- **A speech:** one minute, to a group.
.
**6. Keep one ask.** All three texts ask for the same thing.

Be polite. Be clear. Don’t give up.
body.core:
A **campaign** is an organised effort to change something. The best ones are clear, local and persistent.

**1. Choose an issue.** Pick something real, local and fixable: lighting at the skate park, a later bus, a crossing near school, rubbish in the creek.

**2. Make a specific ask.** “Make the park safer” is vague. “Install two lights at the skate park by winter” is a clear **ask**.

**3. Know your decision-maker.** Who can make the change? The local council, your school principal, a club committee? Your main argument is written for them.

**4. Gather evidence.** Strong campaigns use:
- photos and observations.
- simple surveys (“32 of 40 students said…”).
- facts from reliable sources (council plans, government data).
- real stories from people affected.

**5. Build three texts:**
- **Argument:** a formal letter or opinion piece. State your **point of view**, give two or three reasons with evidence, deal with a **counter-argument**, and finish with your ask.
- **Social post:** a hook, a strong image, the ask, and a call to action (sign the **petition**, share, come to the meeting).
- **Speech:** one minute, to a group or council meeting. A story, the key fact, the ask.
.
**6. Stay consistent.** Same issue, same ask, same name and look across all three.

Change often takes time. Real campaigns can run for years.
body.extend:
A **campaign** is organised advocacy, kept up over time, for one clear change. Most community change comes from campaigns, not single complaints. That is true of new parks and new laws.

**Strategy.**
- **issue:** real, local and specific enough to fix.
- **ask:** exact, achievable and, if you can, with a deadline.
- **decision-maker:** who has the power to act, such as a council, principal, club committee or MP.
- **allies:** people who are affected, or likely to back you.
- **evidence:** photos, surveys, official data and personal stories.

**Texts for different audiences.**
- **A written argument** for the decision-maker. This is a formal letter or opinion piece. It has a clear **point of view**, reasons backed by reliable evidence, a fair answer to a **counter-argument**, and an exact ask.
- **A social post** for supporters. It has a hook, an image, the ask and a call to action, such as a **petition** or event.
- **A speech** for a meeting or assembly. In one minute, it joins a story, evidence and the ask.
.
**Consistency.** Use one name, one look and one ask in every text. That builds trust and momentum.

**Evaluation.** Judge a campaign on results, not just attention. Did the decision-maker act? If so, did the change work as planned? Even winning campaigns often need follow-up.

caseStudies.title: 10 cents a can

body.support:
South Australia has paid people for returning cans and bottles since **1977**. For years, groups in Victoria asked for the same thing.

One group was the **Boomerang Alliance**. It worked with local community groups. They kept asking the government to act.

On **1 November 2023**, Victoria started its own scheme. Now you get **10 cents** back for each can, bottle or carton you return.

The government said it should cut litter in half.

In **2026**, the Boomerang Alliance said the scheme needs to work better. Not enough cans are coming back.

The lesson: campaigns can take years. And after you win, you keep checking.
body.core:
South Australia has had a container deposit scheme since **1977**. People get money back when they return drink containers. For years, campaigners pushed for Victoria to do the same.

The **Boomerang Alliance**, an alliance of environment groups, worked with Victorian community organisations to build pressure. They argued the scheme would cut litter and boost recycling.

On **1 November 2023**, Victoria’s scheme began. People now get a **10-cent** refund for each eligible can, bottle and carton. The government said it expected the scheme to **halve** litter in Victoria.

But the campaign didn’t stop there. In **2026**, the Boomerang Alliance said return rates had stalled at around 65%, and argued the scheme needed improving.

The lesson: a clear ask, repeated over years, can win. But winning the change isn’t the end. You need to check that it works.
body.extend:
South Australia has run a container deposit scheme since **1977**. Victoria was one of the last states to bring one in, after years of advocacy.

The **Boomerang Alliance** is a group of environment organisations. It worked with Victorian community groups to press for a scheme. It argued that a refund would cut litter and lift recycling. It also campaigned on how the scheme was designed. More than 50,000 people signed its petition against drink companies running the scheme.

On **1 November 2023**, Victoria’s scheme began. It pays a **10-cent** refund for each eligible container. The government said it expected the scheme to **halve** litter.

The campaign went on after the win. In **February 2026**, the Boomerang Alliance said return rates had stalled at around 65%. It called for improvements.

The case shows what strong campaigns do. They make a specific ask. They build a group of allies. They keep going for years. They care about the details. And they check the results after the change. It also shows that “winning” and “working” are different tests.

model.text:
**Ask:** install two lights at the Riverside skate park before next winter.
**Letter (opening):** Dear Councillor Lee, I am writing on behalf of young people who use the Riverside skate park. In winter, it is dark by 5:30 pm, so it is unsafe after school. Of 40 skaters we surveyed, 32 said they leave early because of the dark.
**Post:** [Photo: the empty, dark bowl at 6 pm] It’s 6 pm. This is our skate park. Two lights would change everything. Sign the petition (link in bio). #LightUpTheBowl
**Speech (close):** “Two lights. One safer park. We’re asking council to act before winter.”

teacher.overview: A VM 3&4 capstone. Students run a mini campaign on a real local issue: they define the issue, a specific ask and the decision-maker, gather evidence, and produce three linked texts (a formal argument for the decision-maker, a social post for supporters and a one-minute speech), then launch it and evaluate its likely impact. The case study is Victoria’s container deposit scheme: after years of advocacy by the Boomerang Alliance and community groups, it began on 1 November 2023 with a 10-cent refund, and campaigners kept pushing for improvements afterwards.
prep: Find your local council’s contact details and any relevant plans (youth, transport, parks).
Agree a process for sending real letters or posting real petitions (school approval, privacy).
Students should have done some Advocate and Speak Up courses first (this capstone requires two from each).

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 specific local issue; 2 exact, time-bound ask; 3 decision-maker; 4 evidence (photos, survey, council plan); 5 three texts for three audiences; 6 consistent name and look.

**Sort:** strong — official timetable; own survey with numbers; specific personal story. Weak — “everyone hates the bus”; one Facebook comment; a guess of “hundreds”.

**Case study:** campaigners (including the Boomerang Alliance with community groups) pushed for years for a container deposit scheme like South Australia’s (since 1977); Victoria’s began on 1 November 2023 with a 10-cent refund; the government expected litter to halve; in 2026 campaigners said return rates had stalled around 65% and called for improvements. Winning and working are different tests.

realityCheck: **Real campaigns can get real responses.** If letters go to councillors, check them first and prepare students for slow or no replies.
**Keep it civil and local.** Steer students away from personal attacks and towards fixable, specific issues.
**Privacy:** petitions collect names; keep them in class unless there’s a proper process.
**Works in a real class:** yes. A real council reply, even a short one, is a huge motivator.
